title: Understanding Conflict
speaker: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna and Seishu John Wiley
summary: Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna and Seishu John Wiley report on a Whatcom Dispute Center workshop that seven sangha members attended, and they connect its interest and needs based model to the sangha's own ethical guidelines document. Ryushin and Seishu describe the cycle of trigger, escalation, crisis, recovery, and depression, with an early "window" for assessing a situation the way firefighters size up a fire. An iceberg of positions above the water and needs below it is illustrated with two neighbors and a fallen tree, and with two men who settle a dispute over shade and apples. The group reads ten tips and weighs avoiding, competing, compromising, and collaborating, with Congress offered as an example of avoiding. A participant closes by proposing that the quarterly sangha conversations use pre-structured questions to build trust.

And thanks, by the way, to the board and to the sangha for giving us the opportunity to go.
Seven of us were able to be there, so it's really nice that so many of us could attend.

I do want to mention that both John and I had talked about it and really agree that a lot of the information that we got from the Dispute Resolution Center was very compatible with a document that we had developed.
And those of you who aren't familiar with the document.
Yeah, it's ethical guidelines for the [unclear: "Red Seers"] and community practicing with difficulty.

Right.

I think there's about 10 copies back there.
It's good to familiarize yourself with it.
I think it's on our website, too.
Is it?
Maybe?
Yeah, we just rediscovered it, didn't we?
Oh, cool.
Okay.
So we have that.
Business and policies.
Oh, I wanted to say that I was very enthusiastic when I came back.
And for about two weeks I was asking Jeff if we couldn't have a conflict.
At one point I said, "Well, why don't we go out on a date?
If we go out on this date like we used to do before we were married, when we were courting, oh, we could have a conflict.
Wouldn't that be cool?"
He didn't buy into it, but it'll happen.
Believe me, it'll happen.
Since we all feel that we have a pretty benign community, at least we've expressed that before, why are we doing this?
Well, we do have a pretty benign community, really.
We haven't had any major ethical breaches like some of the communities across the country have.
Or any major blowups or any splits.
But people do get frustrated.
And if we are in relationship, if we're human beings, we'll get into conflict eventually at some point.
Certainly there have been frustrations and there have been disagreements, and it's good to address all of this.
The other thing I want to mention is that we have this wonderful gift of sangha as a laboratory where we can practice compassion in this and we can also practice living harmoniously together.
We do share the same values and we have taken the same vows and we have a commitment to end suffering.
So we do have a basis, I think, to trust one another and to feel safe here.
There are some ways, though, we can bump into each other in sangha life.
Edie and I did a role play on this one at one time, if you folks remember.
One area is in the roles and the tasks that we have.
We might find that we need some autonomy perhaps in our role and then somebody else maybe steps in.
Maybe we put something on the website and somebody else changes it or interferes in some way.
So we might get into a conflict or a disagreement that way.
On the other side of that, we might have a project that we're undertaking and we feel like we need some help and the help doesn't show up, like tonight, for example.
That could develop into a conflict.
Or we might not have a conflict with an individual person.
It could be that we don't like the decisions that the practice committee or the board has made, or Tim has made, and we feel conflicted about that.
Or maybe we don't like the decision making process and feel like we could be part of it.
So we have lots of opportunities here.
But I think an important thing to note is that all of our conflicts won't be resolved.
We really can't get everything that we need.
It could just be a personality clash, in which case we have an opportunity here to learn some patience and how to live with each other with equanimity.
A little bit about the model that was presented to us through the Dispute Resolution Center.
It's referred to as an interest and needs based model.
It understands that the perceived needs are at the root of our conflict.
Conflict actually arises from within ourselves, arises internally.
But our habit seems to be that we project it outward.
We tend to attribute it to something external.
It's really more that we feel our strategies, not necessarily our needs, but the strategies to meet the need, are blocked.
They get blocked and then we get frustrated and we clash.
There are other models or other methods for resolution out there, and these aren't the interest based models.
One is a power based model.
In a power based model, it's kind of my way or the highway, and it's often done through threats and coercion.
We see that with our foreign affairs, if we impose a sanction on another country or an embargo, that kind of thing.
Or also in an emergency situation: you call 911, you go to the door and meet the medics, that kind of thing.
So it can be useful in emergencies and actually beneficial.
There are also position based methods, and resolution for those types of methods is usually done through laws, rules or regulations or standards, that kind of thing.
But the goals of this interest based model are really different.
These goals are relational.
The intention is not just to assert our own needs, but also to attend to and understand the needs of the other party.
It's a movement from my goals to our goals.
As I mentioned, it's very compatible with the one that we have in our own document here.
It also understands that conflict does not have to be negative and alienating.
With skills and awareness, it can really lead to greater intimacy and connection.
There was a great deal of material presented in six hours, two three-hour classes.
We just picked three or four different areas that we thought were most important and most interesting.
But there's so much we're not going to be able to cover, so we're just going to touch on a few things.
I'll start with this, which is a typical cycle that someone might go through if they're in a conflict.
I would say we're talking medium to high conflict, not just a mild disagreement with somebody, because those happen all the time and I don't think you would go through a cycle like this.
It starts with a trigger.
That can be a word or a behavior or a situation that pushes our buttons.
When that happens, the body starts to respond.
The heart rate might increase, blood pressure goes up, muscles start to get tense.
Maybe you clench your jaw or make a fist, or you feel tension in your stomach or your shoulders.
And breathing can change.
Breathing can become more rapid or shallow.
Now, we're all different, so different people have different triggers.
One of the things that's highly recommended, both in the class and in our document, is that you learn what your triggers are and when they get activated.
Another thing that happens is blood flow.
If they're activated long enough, blood flow begins to change.

Blood begins to flow to the survival parts of the brain and the body, the big muscles, arms and legs, and away from the cerebral cortex where we do our thinking and to the more instinctual parts of the brain.
So if the triggers go on long enough, you get to the escalation stage, and that's when symptoms start to increase.
There might be at that point sweating, or you might feel frozen: I don't know what to say or do.
Part of the reason that can happen is that when blood flow goes out of the cerebral cortex, it is harder to think.
And then if you go far enough on the escalation stage, it's really hard to come back down.
You have to go this route.
The top of the cycle is crisis.
At that point, maximum blood flow has gone to the survival parts of the body.
The instinctual part of the brain might be thinking, should I run?
Should I hide?
Should I strike out?
Should I yell?
Some kind of a drastic action.
The next one is recovery.
At this point, things are starting to return to the way they were.
Hormones that have been released, like adrenaline, start to be reabsorbed.
The blood flow starts to return to normal.
Breathing might become more relaxed and deeper, and muscles start to relax.
The last stage is depression.
Blood sugar is temporarily depleted, and a person might feel tired or just worn out, and feel some mild physiological depression.
Depending on what happened in the conflict, there can be regret, guilt, that kind of thing.
But I actually found the most interesting part of the whole cycle is here, what I labeled window on either side here.
The instructor might have said balcony.
I wrote down window in my notes, so I'm sticking with window.
But this is a place early in the triggering, you can't use this if you're too far along on the cycle, early in the triggering, to do an assessment.
She used the example of firefighters.
They're trained.
When they show up for a fire, they're going to get triggered by all that's going on there.
They're trained early on to look for this window.
They'll go into a fire and they'll be like, hey, what's burning?
Is it wood?
Is it metal?
Are there people inside the building?
Where are the fire hydrants?
How much hose do we have?
What's the best way to handle this?
That's exactly the opportunity people have early in a conflict, and that is to make an assessment.
In a conflict that might look like: what's the issue here?
Is it important?
Do I need to get involved in it, or can I just let it happen?
What are my needs?
What might the other person's needs be?
What assumptions am I making about the other person?
Maybe: what's the best way to handle this, or what's the best language to use?
If you're able to catch the window, usually it changes the cycle.
The crisis point won't be as high.
The cycle will resolve sooner.
And usually, because you've had a chance to reflect on how to handle a conflict, you'll have a better outcome than if you just react and say or do whatever comes to mind.
And then, as I said before, if you go too far in escalation, you've missed the window.
But it's not too late to decide, I'm taking a little break.

So the recommendation is do something physical to dispel some energy, get away from the situation, give yourself some time to think a little bit about what's going on and what you want to do about it.
And as Kate said, this model fits really well with the material in this.
If you're, for one thing, a regular meditator, undoubtedly you're going to be much more aware of what's happening in your body.
That's certainly one of the things we do on the cushion: just pay attention to the breath, pay attention to how the body feels from head to toe.
If you do that regularly, you'll find that sensitivity happens off the cushion, too.
So it's really handy, much easier to know what your triggers are and when they've gotten activated, when they've escalated.
The other thing that's in this document is a recommend.
We have some parts of it that are recommendations for conflict resolution.
The first part is, before doing anything to resolve a conflict, look at yourself, look at how you're feeling, look at what the issues are for you, what your needs are.
Think about what's going on with the other person.
This fits.
This is exactly what the window is for: to make an assessment, not only of yourself, but of the situation you're in before you take any action.
I know I won't go through all the things that are in this document, but pages seven to eleven have lots of suggestions about how to handle conflict and tips for resolving.
The other thing that's helpful, besides learning what your triggers are and when they get activated, is to know a little bit about your usual style of conflict.
How do you usually handle a conflict when you get into one?
Over time, if you can develop one or two alternatives to that, it just gives you more flexibility, especially if you have a way of handling conflict that doesn't work very well.
There's stuff in here and in our training about that, too.
And I know you're going to talk about that a little bit later tonight.
Styles.
Styles.

I know.
You've got.
Yeah.

What I'm going to do is give you a little scenario, and I'm going to use the same scenario that we used in the workshop.
The issue I'm going to present: there are these two neighbors, and this neighbor's tree is caught in the windfall and lands in this neighbor's property.
This neighbor's position is that you should clean this up and haul it away.
And this neighbor's position is you're going to have your homeowners insurance take care of this.
OK, so those are their positions.
This is what is above, what everybody is aware of when they enter into the conflict.
And then underneath here is this subcategory of interests, what we call interests.
Under there are these hopes, desires, concerns, needs, fears, feelings, really all kinds of stuff sitting below the surface here.
History is here.
But these are the general categories.
So this is our little scenario.
Well, first of all, you might wonder, why is this stuff so important?
It turns out statistically that 80 percent of our conflict is due to misunderstanding.
So that's a heck of a lot of stuff sitting underneath here.
It's the fuel that drives it.
And it's also been shown that if we can increase our understanding and our awareness, then the time and the intensity of the conflict will decrease.
So it's pragmatic, really.
Also, interests are easier to reconcile than positions are.
We get hardened in a position.
It's either yes or no, or black or white.
A lot of times positions are also an "I am" position.
We identify with "I am pro-life," "I am pro-choice," or "I am a liberal, I am a conservative," and we actually begin to form our identity around that.
Those are really harder to break.
So they're broader if we use our interests.
We have more options if we use our interests.
I'll give a little different example.
Let's pretend these two guys have a tree on their boundary, and they're fighting over the tree.
They don't know who's, well, they're arguing over who actually owns this tree.
So this guy over here says, "I'm really interested in the shade from that tree."
And this guy over here says, "Well, I like the apples."
Then they can come together and you can say, "Well, I only need some apples for some pie.
You can have the rest of them."
And the other guy says, "Well, I don't have to really delimit the tree too much, and you can have the shade."
So you can work with it.
That's a real simple example, but you can apply it to more complex situations.
And then if we go a little bit deeper here and start looking at the things down at the bottom, the needs and the fears, we can present or address those needs and fears as universal needs and fears.
I want to say here that in our training, as far as I remember, they really didn't get into universal needs like those of you who have taken any classes in nonviolent communication.
I know you have, and some others of us might have.
They really stress understanding needs as universal: universal needs such as safety, physical or emotional needs, needs for connection, for contribution, needs for beauty, rest.
So, the things that we can all identify with.
And actually, I did put a list up there from the nonviolent communication people.
It's just a brief one.
They have really long, extensive ones if you want to look at that or pick that up when you're done here.
But what's important about making these universal?
Well, it seems kind of obvious: if we relate to our needs this way and we share them in that manner, then we also have a sense of our common humanity.
We have a sense of our sameness, and we can become more sensitive to one another and feel more empathy for one another.
So we can begin our confluent resolution on that basis.
They also help us to understand that we're mutually responsible for solving this problem.
And eventually we will address more specific needs as time goes on in the procedure.
I was thinking about this, too: it also takes some willingness in the process to be transparent and vulnerable.
And Mary was saying, that's the teacher, she was saying that often our needs and fears down here at the bottom of this little iceberg, people tend to feel reluctant about expressing them.
She's done like 20 years of conflict resolution.
She's seen this over time, and there seems to be some hesitancy.
But I think it's important to consider this vulnerability and transparency, particularly if the relationship is more intimate and we're committed to it.
It's going to be a longer range.
So we want to be able to really increase our understanding of those kinds of relationships.
But sometimes we may not feel safe, or we may not trust each other well enough.
If trust is not at a maximum, we can take the opportunity to get to know the person better over time.
We can take the whole process just step by step, and a little slower than we might want to.

We can also really begin to have more compassion for our own needs, and understand those a little bit better and examine them more deeply, if we're not yet able to really share that with the other person.
So OK, now we're moving on to the next step, which would be to identify with this other fellow over here what concerns we have that are mutual.
In this particular scenario, they're probably both interested in having a neighborly relationship, or they may be interested in safety.
This thing has fallen over the other guy's yard and kids are playing in it, so they might be concerned about that.
They may be concerned about the financial outlay that they have.
Now that they've acknowledged one another, and they've also acknowledged that they even share their interests, the positions are softened.
Hopefully they won't rise up to the top of that arc that John was showing you, at the top of that bell curve.
So now you're ready to begin some tradeoffs in the process.
It's ideal to begin with some lower-grade tradeoffs.
In this case, maybe you can trade the firewood off, or maybe "I'm willing to pay a third of the cost," or "I'll help you chop the wood," or something like that.
You may find that your conflict is over at that point.
But if you still haven't reached it, or you've still decided on a harder bottom line, at least you're in a position to not blow up.
Usually, we hope so, after going through this process.
The idea, through the whole process, is to stay curious and to continue listening to the other partner.
How am I doing?
Am I talking too long, John?
**Seishu John Wiley:** I was thinking we forgot to mention we're happy to take questions as we go.
So if you have any now or as we go along, just raise your hand.

At first you think this sounds really corny or really artificial, but it really helps.
John's talking about these old brains, the reptilian and the mammalian brains.
To really get over that fight or flight response or reaction, we have to do a lot of training.
It's OK if we fail or if we fight or if we embarrass ourselves or embarrass the other person.
It's OK because it's really a learning opportunity that we have.
We can begin to acknowledge and recognize where we might be falling short.
And we can also become aware of where we might have hurt or offended the other person.
In so doing, we can express our regrets and apologize.
I don't mean to grovel about it, but a sincere apology really goes a long way in mending relationships.
And it is an indication of weakness.
Oh, can I say one more?
There's this other study.
I don't know where I found it, because I didn't know I'd be talking about this at the time.
But there was a study done of business executives.
They were surveying their attitudes toward conflict in the workplace and how they dealt with it.
Eighty-five percent of them said they avoided conflict in the workplace, or confronting these issues in the organization.
They didn't want to appear weak or that they weren't in control, or they just felt that they didn't have the time.
So I think we want to be aware of what the consequences are when we have a question.

**Participant:** Is that to say that they avoid conflict between, like, they're the managers, they're avoiding the conflict amongst the people they're managing, or they themselves try to just not conflict with anyone?
**Ryushin Kate Korn McKenna:** I think it was just in general, either their own peers and supervisors or people that they were managing.
They mentioned that they didn't want to get embroiled, and also this factor of time.
Yeah.
So like I said, I would have paid more attention if I thought I was going to talk about it.
But, I don't know.

It seems to me like maybe, wouldn't you think people sometimes avoid conflict because they've always decided that the other person is wrong? [unclear: "That's why you love them."] Yeah, that's a thought.
But, I don't know.
Maybe there's more incentive to go head to head in a conflict when you do think the other person is wrong.
I think that's more what it is.
Yeah.
But I want to mention the consequence.
The consequence of not taking the time and not doing it is that people leave the organization.
So I think it's really important to remember that here with us.
If we are ever tempted or considering avoiding a conflict, remember what those consequences are and ask ourselves if we've really let it go.
It's important to really let it go.
Otherwise it just festers with people and builds up, and then if they don't feel like there's an open environment for it, they just leave.
So that's it on this item.
Do you want to do the tips for resolving conflict or the styles of conflict?
Maybe since we know what we're doing with that, why don't we do this?
Well, we've got handouts, tips for resolving conflict, and maybe each person can read one and pass it on to the next person.
*One is stay curious.
It's important to remind yourself to respect yourself.
Curiosity leads to more understanding, learning and growth.
It helps you get to the bottom of the iceberg.
Remember, wherever there is conflict, there is opportunity.*
*Two, recognize your own triggers and respect those of others.
It is important to become aware of what your own triggers are as well as to learn more about what triggers those around you.
The more awareness you have for yourself, the better able you are to learn how to respond positively.*
*Three, recognize your own physical responses.
Remember that our bodies can respond very quickly when triggered and also give us extraordinary clues about our own well-being.
It's also essential to be aware of the responses of others and to not make assumptions.*
*Four, recognize when you are escalating and when you need to step away.
Because our quality of judgment declines as our emotion and adrenaline escalates, we have to train ourselves to step away and de-escalate before engaging in important conversations.*
*Five, be intentional and deliberate in your communication.
Think about what you want to achieve and what will get you there.
We often lose sight of this when we have escalated.
Reminding ourselves and others that we want a positive outcome and that we don't want to fight will help shape our communication.*
*Six, use language that will minimize the possibility of defensiveness.
Since we can only control ourselves, we must remember to speak from our own experience and to not use blaming or criticizing language.
Focusing on behavior and not people keeps the topic neutral and not personal.*
**Seishu John Wiley:** *Seven, recognize when someone else is escalated and identify if and how you are contributing.
You may not be escalated, but if the other person is, it may not be a good time to have those important conversations.
Consider what you might do to help them.
Reflect, reframe, clarify.
Eight, focus on needs, whether they are psychological, procedural, or physical, etc.
Nine, be thoughtful when choosing the when and where to discuss a conflict.
Neutral, safe locations can help the conversation stay productive.
Number ten is listen.*
Kate and I thought that should be put in between every number.
If you're not listening, you're not going to work anything out.
I think that's the most important thing of all.
This is the part of the presentation that neither Kate and I prepared for, but we thought it was important.

In the class we went over different styles of conflict, and we thought we could maybe take a look at each one, and people could volunteer what the advantages and disadvantages of each style of conflict are.
So the first one is avoiding.
Any advantages, Tim?

On the bad side, you may not get to a resolution of the issue, and it just sort of sits around and you get back to it.
